newsitem.title: USA: Commuter carrier grounds flights - FAA.
newsitem.headline: Commuter carrier grounds flights - FAA.

text.p: A commuter carrier for United and Midway Airlines grounded flights after federal inspectors found it operated "unairworthy aircraft," the Federal Aviation Administration said Saturday.

Great Lakes Aviation Ltd, based in Spencer, Iowa, voluntarily agreed to suspend operations on Friday after the FAA told the carrier it planned to suspend its operating authority, the aviation agency said in a statement.
"The FAA does not hesitate to take swift action to protect the safety of the flying public," said Barry Valentine, acting FAA administrator.

The company operates as Great Lakes Airlines and, under agreements with United Airlines and Midway Airlines, as United Express and Midway Connection. It runs 500 flights a day carrying about 887,000 passengers annually, FAA said.
Company officials were not immediately available for comment.

FAA said it stepped up surveillance of Great Lakes' maintenance operations on April 29 after findings by its Des Moines office. It said it found the airline allowed personnel who were not properly trained and qualified to perform aircraft maintenance.
"The FAA alleges that the airline operated unairworthy aircraft," the statement said.
Great Lakes Aviation has a fleet of 53 twin-engine turboprop aircraft. It offers service to 82 cities across the U.S. and three cities in Mexico.
Passengers were advised to call their travel agent or the airline.

The FAA said its action was not related to last November's accident in Quincy, Ill., when a Great Lakes-operated United Express plane collided with a small aircraft killing 14 people. It was Great Lakes' first crash in more than 20 years of operation.

Last month, the company reported a net loss for 1996 of $12.8 million, due in part to a special charge of $1.5 million to write down the value of its spare parts inventory. In March, Great Lakes said it was experiencing liquidity difficulties and in talks with creditors.
